newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - IMPORTS TO PUSH UP JULY PPI.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - IMPORTS TO PUSH UP JULY PPI.

text.p: Producer inflation is expected to have succumbed to a variety of pressures in July, notably costlier imports, economists said on Friday.

A Reuters poll of nine economists forecast the producer price index (PPI) would rise 0.8 percent month-on-month in July or 6.6 percent year-on-year, compared with a 0.7 and 6.1 percent increase in June.
The data will be released on Monday at 0900 GMT.
Economists said that the major threat to producer inflation in July was likely to be the effects of higher imported prices following the rand's 25 percent depreciation this year.
"My major fear is that a lot of the push (in July) will come from imported inflation," said Econometrix economist Tony Twine.

Sanlam senior economist Pieter Calitz expected the imported component of PPI, which has a weighting of just under 20 percent, to rise 6.4 percent from July last year compared with a 4.7 percent rise in June.

Frankel Pollak bond analyst Tertia Jacobs expected, however, that the roughly two-month lag effect of declining crude oil prices in April and May would offset the effects of other rising imported prices.

"Crude oil prices peaked in mid-April at about $22.50 a barrel then came down to a low of about $18 a barrel in mid-May," Jacobs said. "That could partially offset other rising imported prices and higher food prices," she said.
One economist noted that July was traditionally a high survey month.
"The fall in the rand that we saw between April and July will be captured in some of the categories that are surveyed quarterly," the economist said.
She also said that some of the categories surveyed in July, such as petroleum and coal products and chemicals and chemical products, had reasonably high weightings in the overall index.
SMK Securities economist Herman van Papendorp said other categories surveyed in the month included tobacco, beverages, wood products, pulp and paper, leather and rubber and plastics.
He said that another factor which would place upward pressure on the PPI was food prices.
"We have seen in the CPI that food pressures are starting to mount and I think this is going to be shown in both agricultural and manufacturing food products," van Papendorp said.
In July, the annual rate of increase in consumer food prices was at its highest since July 1995, rising 4.8 percent year-on-year -- 2.3 percentage points higher than in June.

Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes, noted that technical factors would also play their part. PPI rose just 0.3 percent in July 1995, which would mean the latest data would be calculated off a low base.

"One mustn't ignore the fact that at this stage last year the PPI rate was dropping like a stone, and when it stops dropping it causes an arithmetic effect which is not always that pleasant," Econometrix's Twine said.
Speculation about a U.S. interest rate rise after Friday's robust August payroll report looks set to dominate economic markets in the week ahead, analysts in London said.

Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International, said the market focus this week would be on the remaining pieces of economic data which the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will have in front of it when it meets on September 24.
These include July consumer credit figures on Monday, the Beige book on U.S. economic conditions on Wednesday, August consumer and producer prices on Thursday and August retail sales on Friday.
Edmonds said the focus in Europe would be on budget preparations in countries including France, Sweden, Spain and the Netherlands.
The main concern here was whether budgets were credible and consistent with the Maastricht Treaty on European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Sean Shepley, international economist at Credit Suisse First Boston, said British inflation numbers due out this week were likely to stay muted, but probably would not be as benign as in previous months, especially Monday's producer prices for August.

Shepley said that in France, August CPI on Friday should continue a downtrend in its annual rate, especially since the increase in value-added tax in August 1995 would now drop out of the latest 12-month period.

Shepley said that no official news was expected out of the European Union's monetary committee meeting starting in Brussels on Monday but markets would pay close attention to preparations for the September 20-21 meeting of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin.
On the back of that meeting, he said some people were looking for an easing of German interest rates and possibly a statement of Franco-German solidarity on EMU.
In Japan, Shepley said markets would continue to focus on rumours about an October election and also the possibility of a supplementary budget.
Mark Capleton, international bond strategist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd, said it was a fairly sparse week for data on continental Europe.
Capleton said there would be some interest in Spain's CPI figure for August which is due from Thursday.

Capleton forecast French August CPI, due out on Friday, would be flat for the month and rise 1.9 percent year-on-year. In Britain, Capleton foresaw a small fall in output price inflation at 1.3 percent year-on-year to August from 1.5 percent year-on-year in July.
